Our findings demonstrate that our nanoantenna array meets the criteria for being an active, all-dielectric metamaterial. Furthermore, we show through simulations that the spectral positions of resonances can be independently adjusted via changes in nanogap size, and also through external applied electric fields. This offers a possibility for our nanoantenna array to be integrated into larger photonic systems, enabling control of optical diffraction signals using laser light to trigger chemical reactions within tiny fluid volumes.

Our investigation into the plasticity phenomenon in glassy amorphous materials, like broken ceramics and molten metals, focuses on developing a microscopic understanding through molecular dynamics simulations. We've identified that, at low temperatures, structural rearrangements within these materials occur through rare, spontaneous energy fluctuations. We've modeled this by creating a'micro-crack' in a'membrane model' to study, finding that micro-cracks amplify localized stress concentrations that lower the material's mechanical strength, increasing its susceptibility to plasticity. In contrast, crystalline solids exhibit significantly higher mechanical strength. This difference is attributed to the ordered crystal's ability to distribute and absorb more effectively the elastic energy generated by internal defects, whereas the disordered glass lacks this ability, leading to an increased propensity for plasticity in its absence.

Research on a four-band Hubbard model using tight-binding for silicene monolayers with adsorbed Mn atoms at different substitutional sites has been conducted. Calculations showed that replacing Mn at sublattice sites A or B with H or F atoms results in varying onsite interaction strengths, with A site modifications exhibiting weaker interactions and B site modifications exhibiting stronger interactions. These differences may influence the phase diagram of the electronic correlation and the resulting phase transitions. Additionally, our findings can guide experimental procedures for producing silicene-Mn systems through chemical decoration.

The galactic center region contains multiple massive radio sources, including the pulsar-circled Sgr A East supernova remnant (SNR). This paper examines X-ray data from Chandra and NuSTAR observations, allowing for more precise measurements of their sizes and shapes. Due to their proximity to the galactic center, researchers used a novel method incorporating the effects of galactic bulge light to accurately determine their distances. This approach also takes into account the distribution of young stars and other galactic structures to confirm the previously estimated distance of 280 parsecs for Sgr A East, with an uncertainty of 20 parsecs. Further analysis of X-ray spectra from Chandra observations revealed the presence of two plasma components, indicating a significant discrepancy between light elements and heavy elements. This was observed in the north-west and south-west quadrants of the SNR, with the north-west region showing higher levels of heavy elements. This asymmetry is believed to be caused by either a shock wave from Sgr A* or the effects of a galactic wind. Additionally, researchers found evidence of radiative acceleration affecting X-ray emission from Sgr A East, with X-ray emission from the south-west quadrants being directed towards the earth due to this effect. This is consistent with a shock wave model, with shock waves from Sgr A* potentially explaining observed polarimetry data and the lack of a central source within Sgr A East, as well as its similarity to SNR G0.06

The prevalence of data with class imbalance, featuring an uneven number of instances per class, poses significant challenges to machine learning algorithms. In particular, popular methods tend to suffer lower accuracy and instability when dealing with highly skewed data. Notably, studies have demonstrated that state-of-the-art neural networks are more resilient to data imbalance issues but have not extensively investigated their performance under various data distributions. This study aims to bridge this gap by conducting a comprehensive comparison of well-known algorithms (KNN, SVM, and neural networks) under extreme class imbalance conditions. Our research reveals that while neural networks perform relatively well across all datasets, other algorithms struggle, with KNN exhibiting the lowest results. Interestingly, undersampling the majority class leads to the smallest differences in performance across the three algorithms. These findings suggest that undersampling the majority class is a more effective strategy to mitigate class imbalance issues.

This study examines how local news in the US covered the COVID-19 pandemic from its initial outbreak in 2020 to spring 2021. Utilizing a dataset of 250,000 articles from 200 sources, we analyzed the output of 10 major newspapers and 190 smaller publications to gain insight into volume fluctuations, topic trends, and geographic disparities. Our results indicate significant differences in local news coverage, with state-specific topics and frequencies emerging, as well as varying responses to vaccination milestones. Moreover, we discovered shifts in topic emphasis, with certain issues like school reopenings gaining more attention as the pandemic ebbed. These findings hold important implications for audiences, journalists, and advertisers.

In near-field scenarios of the Fast Multipole Method, the computational cost can be
excessive due to the quadratic complexity of the matrix-Vector products in the outer
clusters, which can hinder the FMM's efficiency in space-time simulations of gravitational
phenomena over long periods of time. To address these near-field costs, we've developed
an innovative strategy that reduces the FMM's overall time expenditure in such applications.
This approach initially identifies near-field interactions and then applies a hierarchical
cluster scheme to further pinpoint those matrix-Vector products that can be minimized.
By substituting these eliminable matrix-Vector products with more computationally
efficient operations such as BLAS-3 and BLAS-1, we can significantly reduce the FMM's
overall time expenditure. This strategy has been thoroughly analyzed, tested, and applied
in a space-time simulation of a black hole merger, yielding substantial gains in the FMM's
efficiency.

The $e$-$p$-$e$-$p$ double Compton scattering process at the Large Hadron Collider has been examined to determine its potential for accessing unique information about PDFs and assessing the proton's polarization. By analyzing the differential cross sections and double spin asymmetries within the $e$-$e$ system, where one electron is inelastic scattered and the other remains initial, the dependence on the proton's polarization can be evaluated. Given the LHC's high luminosity, the method may offer a means to directly determine PDFs over a wide range in $x$ corresponding to $x\approx 10^{-3}-10^{-5}$ with errors limited by the measurement precision.

Highly complex control problems, especially those with numerous degrees of freedom, have long been difficult to address using reinforcement learning due to their extensive action space. This action space is typically too large for such learning methods to be efficient. As a result, experts often rely on search algorithms to discover optimal control policies, which are then difficult or nearly impossible to replicate using reinforcement learning. A novel technique, augmented policy cloning, offers a potential solution by learning an auxiliary function aiding policy transfer. We successfully applied this method to transfer complex robotic behaviors from expert to student policies. In a test involving a challenging 12-DoF Red Dragon arm, our approach allowed the student policy to master tasks originally developed by an expert using search algorithms. This achievement was accompanied by a significant reduction in training time for the student policy, whose reinforcement learning-based training took roughly 20 times less time than the original expert training. Our results show promising potential for augmented policy cloning in robotic applications.

Investigations of Higgs boson production via gluon fusion have been carried out at the Large Hadron Collider using data collected with the ATLAS and CMS detectors, amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions. Analyzing these data, the presence of additional high-energy particles was investigated to examine Higgs boson decays into the Standard Model final states $b\bar{b}$ and $W^+ W^-$. Utilizing a frequentist method to calculate confidence intervals, the results revealed that certain resonance forms, contributing to Higgs boson production via loop interference, are disfavored by the data at more than five standard deviations for mass ranges 500 to 850 GeV for a heavy scalar and 200 to 600 GeV for a pseudoscalar. These findings are consistent with previous findings from the LHC's 7 and 8 TeV data and with theoretical predictions for vector boson fusion and vector boson associated production.

In the 1950s, masers based on resonant spin ensembles became pivotal tools for scientific research, used extensively to study the interstellar medium and measure magnetic fields. Over the past twenty years, a new generation of masers has been developed by employing digital signal processing techniques to analyze resonant spin responses. This would have been an impossible task without the integration of high-speed, yet highly noise-introducing digital signal processing. This thesis delves into the theoretical limits of digital signal processing noise in maser systems and presents practical methods to minimize this noise to levels compatible with resonant spin maser applications. This is achieved by employing signal processing algorithms on a field-programmable gate array in conjunction with a coherent magnetometer that senses magnetic field fluctuations.

We've developed new methods for analyzing hypergeometric groups arising from the Lefschetz hyperplane section formula, specifically in the context of K3 surfaces. This has led us to identify certain hypergeometric groups as arithmetic subgroups of the K3 surface's Picard group, and we've established a new approach for generating a maximal arithmetic subgroup from a given curve's moduli. Furthermore, we've derived new classifications for hypergeometric groups, linking them to the shape of the Lefschetz transform, and offering insights into the Luttinger transformations. Additionally, our research explores how hypergeometric groups can be applied to the study of K3 surface automorphisms, examples of which include the HPD triangle case, Sawada's K3 surface, and the Dodeca Tate shape.

We propose a novel, yet-to-be-excluded signature for detecting dark matter particles, where a neutralino decays into a neutralino and a gamma ray, and suggest a experimental setup to capture this process at high-altitude particle detectors such as IceCube. The decay of interest involves the production of a relativistic gamma ray, where the energy is sufficient to traverse the ice before being recorded by multiple detectors simultaneously, thus enabling the reconstruction of the track direction. The proposed method utilizes the ice itself as an optical channel to pinpoint the decay location, thereby facilitating the identification of the neutralino's mass. With an annual exposure of approximately $10^9$\,g$\cdot$year, IceCube has the sensitivity to rule out neutralino masses up to 500\,GeV for a wide range of hidden sector coupling values.

The genus of a graph represents the minimum number of surface embeddings required. A well-known upper bound, established by Nash-Williams and Ellis, can be expressed as the sum of the genus and a specific combination of the clique number and the minimum number of crossings in a graph's representation. Although this bound has been shown to be tight for certain types of graphs, a more precise bound has been discovered for $K_{p, d + p}$ with a specified condition on $d$. This new bound is a function of the genus, $p$, and $d$.

In many stochastic optimization problems, such as those encountered in statistical learning, online matching, and queueing analysis, the convergence rate is often established under the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data sequences. Recent studies have explored ways to reduce the number of communication rounds in these optimization methods, and this paper summarizes the key advancements in this area. Several strategies for achieving faster convergence rates without requiring additional assumptions about data structures are presented, and some special cases involving diversification and localized analysis are discussed in more detail.

Our research focuses on developing a NER model for the Hebrew language by leveraging progress made in NER tasks on other Hebrew models. We begin by training a Hebrew transformer model using data from various sources, including NER tasks performed by other Hebrew models. We then enable cross-lingual transfer by training our model on data from multiple Hebrew sources, ensuring it meets NER requirements. We assess our model's effectiveness using precise and f1 metrics. We also investigate other training methods, such as initial small-scale training, to improve our model's performance. We discovered that initial small-scale training and cross-lingual transfer can effectively train a Hebrew model without extensive data. Moreover, our model's performance is comparable to leading Hebrew NER models. We also found that initial small-scale training and cross-lingual transfer can successfully adapt a model to new languages, such as Modern Hebrew and Ashkenazi Hebrew. We believe our work can serve as a foundation for future studies on Hebrew NER.

The performance of the current GTPC detector concept is evaluated in terms of its ability to differentiate between electron and nuclear recoils at low energies using new detection techniques.  By analyzing data from the DarkSide-50 experiment, it has been found that two newly introduced observables can surpass the rejection capabilities of time-dependent ionization multivariate analysis parameters.  By combining these observables with existing ionization models, scientists can create an even more advanced single-parameter measurement.  Calculations predict how effective these observables and combinations are at various recoil velocities, indicating they have great potential for improving the detection capabilities of the experiment.  Predictions also show that the entire GTPC detector can achieve comparable or even better discrimination abilities than the DarkSide-50 detector, even at the lowest energies.

Driver behavior assessment is a significant factor in operating driving-assistance systems and navigating traffic efficiently. Currently, driver behavior evaluation is typically done solely by the vehicle's sensors, which might not always have access to relevant external traffic information. Including expert feedback can provide more comprehensive insights, but doing so regularly can be impractical. To address these limitations, this research proposes a solution that enables vehicles to obtain and integrate both internal driver state data and external traffic conditions through wireless connectivity, ultimately allowing for more informed driver behavior assessment. The efficacy of this proposed system was demonstrated in a real-world driving experiment, which showed that incorporating traffic data alongside driver state improves the accuracy of driver behavior analysis under varying external driving conditions with feedback from expert drivers.

Recent advancements in scene text recognition models have been notable, with open-source benchmarks like ICDAR2013 RRC playing a crucial role in driving progress. The benchmark's "Scene" dataset, particularly, has been instrumental in this endeavor, with its Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) section standing out as a particularly challenging part. The prominence of "Scene" and its OOV dataset has led to the creation of several highly-performing models. However, a closer examination of the dataset's models and evaluations has revealed a concerning lack of robustness testing, particularly for infrequent and uncommon words. To address this gap, this research paper proposes a more effective evaluation protocol for open-set scene text recognition models. The proposed method is based on a simple idea: words not seen during training should not be predicted by the model. By adopting this protocol, the evaluation of models on the "Scene" dataset yields significantly different rankings than the traditional IFTT+WT method. Furthermore, the proposed protocol yields comparable performance on frequent words but better handles the infrequent ones. The experimental results also highlight the need for novel evaluation protocols that accurately reflect the real-world performance of models.

Two random fields, each describing different spatial patterns of variability, can be compared by measuring the logarithmic complexity of their spatial patterns of variability. This is achieved by quantifying the similarity between two random fields, each characterized by a specific scaling regime. To compare such fields, we first determine the optimal scaling regime that best describes the variability patterns of each field, and then calculate the logarithmic complexity of the optimal fields for each, before computing the similarity metric as the difference in their complexity values. This approach is applicable to any random field, whether it be Gaussian or non-Gaussian, and whether its variability pattern exhibits self-similarity at various scales. Comprehensive numerical simulations have been performed to validate this approach for Gaussian fields, while its potential applicability to non-Gaussian fields remains a topic for future research.

The technique of magnetic levitation is used to suspend a ferromagnetic fluid or solid in the midst of a laboratory experiment. This method is utilized in both stationary and flowing systems, including levitating fluids within another flowing stream or on a moving plate. The presence of magnetic levitation introduces an unusual element, as it introduces additional factors such as magnetic forces and moments that affect the dynamics of the system. In this tutorial, we provide an overview of the fundamental principles involved in magnetic levitation and offer an analytical framework to assess its influence on the dynamics of the system under investigation. The tutorial also delves into the specific details of two experiments, namely, levitating fluids within another flowing stream and moving plate studies, with a focus on how magnetic levitation can significantly impact the system's dynamics, both in the vicinity of the levitated object and at larger scales.

A key tool in understanding the long-term behavior of individual Hecke L-functions near 1 is the partial integral formula derived by Bagchi and Saha. Leveraging this formula, recent qualitative results regarding SL2(Z) Hecke L-functions have been achieved. This research extends some of these results to Hecke L-functions of Spn(Z) eigenforms, revealing similarities and differences with their SL2(Z) counterparts. Notably, some results are obtainable from the partial integral formula, while other outcomes necessitate a novel analysis of the rate of growth of Spn(Z) Hecke eigenforms.

To study how graphene and normal conductor patches are connected, we develop a comprehensive technique for calculating the electrical characteristics of junctions between graphene and normal conductors. By using this method, we can accurately determine the transmission rates of charge and energy, as well as the influence of the junction on the spin and energy transport. The tool allows for the calculation of the spin Hall effect and energy flux in graphene and normal conductors by integrating the transmission rates over energy and momentum. The technique can handle complex geometries by solving the wave equations independently for graphene and normal conductors and combining the solutions at the interface between the two materials. The method can be applied to a wide range of junction geometries, including those with different shapes and sizes, and can also be used to study the transport of heat and charge in three-dimensional systems.

This study establishes conditions for the convergence of weakly convergent sequences within Banach lattices by employing the combination of the reiteration theorem and the principle of the maximum, along with the properties of locally Lipschitz functions and weakly nonlinear operators. It reveals that the effect of weak nonlinearity and monotony in locally Lipschitz functions depends on the specific norm used, differentiating between uniformly convex and smooth norms. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that, within the context of Banach lattices, the conditions of the theorem are neither universally applicable nor unnecessarily restrictive.

Our research builds upon existing results by establishing a direct connection between independent vertex sets and pancyclic components. This connection allows us to derive pancyclic subgraph results, which in turn enable us to determine the minimum pancyclic vertex count for graph G given its independent vertex set count and maximum degree δ. When δ = 2, we've found that the independent vertex set count must be at least n/3 for graph G to possess a pancyclic subgraph of size at least n/6. When δ ≥ 3, we've found that the independent vertex set count must be at least (3k^2 + k + 4)/18 for graph G to possess a pancyclic subgraph of size at least k. When δ = 3 and k is 8 or larger, we've found that the independent vertex set count must be at least n/3 for graph G to possess a pancyclic subgraph of size at least n/9. When δ is 4 or larger and k is 5 or larger, we've found that the independent vertex set count must be at least n/5 for pancyclic subgraph of size k^2/(δ - 1) + k/2 - 2. When δ is 5, we've found that the independent vertex set count must be at least n/5 for pancyclic subgraph of size 10.

The initial conditions of the quark gluon plasma play a significant role in understanding its medium properties. In this study, we analyze how various Transverse flow effects influence the flow pattern in the momentum space, particularly under Central and Aligned conditions. The results show that a Transverse profile creates irregular initial medium properties, resulting in irregular pressure gradients and increased flow velocities of light hadrons. This, in turn, affects the distribution of particles in the Transverse direction, particularly rapidity-dependent anisotropic flows. The effects of Transverse profiles on flow properties are more pronounced than those caused by Aligning effects, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

A new high-performance approach called SASK has been developed to efficiently solve diverse PDEs with boundary and interface conditions. This algorithm models PDE solutions as sums of fundamental solutions, whose locations are adjusted to account for inhomogeneities and boundary data. The approach employs an adaptive mesh that is refined via an error estimator, built upon a hierarchical representation of the inhomogeneities and boundary data. This robust framework allows for seamless treatment of multiple and countably infinite families of inhomogeneities and boundary data. The implementation details of the algorithm can be tailored to accommodate various acoustics, electrostatics, and other PDE scenarios. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated by numerical results for the Helmholtz, Laplace, and biharmonic equations in two and three dimensions.

We employ the spectroscopic method based on the bound-variational method to study a water molecule under the influence of an external DC electric field. We calculate a range of vibrational and rotational constants for the $0\rightarrow 1$ excitation in both the fundamental and first fundamental states as the electric field strength varies from 0 to 100 D. Our results demonstrate consistency with existing literature on the resonance parameters for the fundamental state but provide longer-term predictions for the associated rotational levels and vibrational modes. Furthermore, our calculations yield accurate ro-vibrational energy patterns for both the fundamental and first fundamental states as the electric field increases. Our approach relies on a highly efficient and accurate approximation technique, yielding a significant reduction in computational complexity, enabling us to achieve these outcomes with relatively few basis set components.

The Sinkhorn algorithm was originally developed for solving optimal transport, specifically for finding the most cost-effective way to distribute a discrete probability distribution. This distribution is referred to as a "sinkhorn iterate." In our research, we examine the relationship between sinkhorn algorithm iterates and the solutions to a discrete Schrödinger equation. Our findings indicate that as the Sinkhorn algorithm approaches a solution to the dual of the Sinkhorn problem (either an optimal solution or a limiting point), the corresponding sinkhorn iterates converge to a discrete eigenfunction of the Schrödinger operator. Notably, if there is no solution to the Schrödinger problem, the sinkhorn iterates converge to a discrete eigenfunction that does not exist in the classical sense. Our study focuses on the Sinkhorn algorithm in its original form, which relies on clamping. To demonstrate the utility of our results, we apply them to a research study on the properties of clamped eigenfunctions, which are solutions to a family of related Schrödinger equations with a clamping parameter.

Measurements of the cross-section of top-quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy are reported. The data, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb^-1, was recorded with the CMS detector at the LHC. The measurements are based on the data from a defined energy range and are provided for the total cross-section as well as separate states, considering the presence or absence of a lepton. The results are compared with the predictions of quantum chromodynamics, based on next-to-leading order calculations at a fixed order in perturbation theory, and are also compared with the predictions of the next-to-leading order perturbative QCD at the next-to-leading order in the strong interaction. The predictions are provided through the automated code MCFM and include various corrections for the final state. The measurements are provided after a correction for the residual systematic uncertainty and are compared with the predictions, providing a good agreement with the data. The data, reported in terms of the differential cross-section, are also compared with the predictions, showing a good agreement with the data. The measurements are also provided in terms of the transverse momentum distribution of the top quarks and the differential cross-section, allowing for further comparison with the predictions.

We investigate the dynamics of quantum correlations within a disordered systems of interacting spins under the influence of repeated projective measurements on a central qubit or cavity mode connected to it. Beyond initial rapid fluctuations, the results reveal the coexistence of long-term entanglement between the central element and the surrounding heat bath. This phenomenon arises due to the slowing of dephasing processes by the discrete spectrum of a central cavity or qubit and the periodic nature of measurement events. The findings are highly relevant for analyzing the quantum nature of thermal fluctuations in pre-thermal phases and their utilization in central element-based quantum technologies.

This research investigates several key characteristics such as Janowski convexity, Janowski convexity with respect to a convex function, and Sierpi\'nski convexity of the generalized Bessel function of order $\lambda$, defined as $G_{\lambda}(z)$, and the generalized Mittag-Leffler function of order $\alpha$, initially introduced by F. G. Garrao \& A. Tom\'as, in the unit disk $|z| < 1$. They also explore several distinct classes of functions tied to $G_{\lambda}(z)$. The study utilizes the function $f(z) = 1 + \frac{2a(z)}{1-z}$, where $|a(z)| < 1$, to illustrate functions that are not of Normann class $A$ but are of class $S_{M}$, in addition to identifying specific conditions under which $G_{\lambda}(z)$ is of class $S_{M}$. Furthermore, they determine conditions under which $G_{\lambda}(z)$ is starlike in the unit disk $|z| < 1$. The research also assesses the efficiency of the theorem of Sierpi\'nski convexity, in the context of $G_{\lambda}(z)$, and identifies conditions under which $G_{\lambda}(z)$ is Sierpi\'nski convex in the unit disk $|z| < 1$. The study also

The COVID-19 pandemic marked a significant turning point for humanity in the 21st century, with far-reaching consequences still being felt today. In the midst of the global health crisis, our research explores the broader social impact and resilience of urban communities. Utilizing mobile sensor data from over 500,000 individuals in over 200 countries and territories, our study examines how diverse cultures around the world adapted to the crisis between April 2020 and April 2021. Our findings reveal a notable shift towards more homogeneous social environments, with individuals limiting their interactions to closer, familiar groups. In the long-term, this reduced diversity in urban encounters has resulted in decreased community resilience. Interestingly, our data show that countries with lower diversity in urban environments prior to the pandemic were less affected by the crisis, whereas those with higher diversity were better equipped to mitigate its social impacts. These insights not only shed light on the intricate relationship between mobility, diversity, and community resilience during times of crisis but also highlight the importance of preserving urban diversity as a means of enhancing societal resilience.

The FSMSN algorithm, an iterative method for multi-component energy and mass transport, has been developed to improve speed and energy efficiency over time. It uses a sequential approach to fully implicit solutions, which can be inefficient due to repeated iterations per time step. In contrast, FSMSN reduces the maximum number of iterations. Although both methods converge to the same point, our simulations show FSMSN converging faster and using less energy. As a result, it's a more efficient option. We've also found that using FSMSN in conjunction with fully implicit temperature and mass conservation equations yields better performance. When comparing FSMSN to accelerating fully implicit and sequential solutions in oil recovery simulations, we found FSMSN took 30% less time. However, FSMSN wasn't faster in another simulation. Our study shows that accelerating fully implicit can still be a faster approach under certain conditions.

The development of optical cavities that interact specifically with left- or right-handed light is crucial for advancing research in the unique properties of chiral materials. A new, single-handedness chiral optical cavity concept has been developed that enhances interactions between specific chiral emitters and light. By combining two handpicked mirror materials, the cavity achieves single-handedness and amplifies interactions with all surrounding emitters through an amplified spin Hall effect. The single-handedness and cavity mode amplification are protected against misalignment, scattering, and temperature variations. The cavity has optimal performance with emitters in close proximity and high spatial confinement, which can be fine-tuned through the cavity's dimensions. The concept was demonstrated in a GaAs wafer, which is known for its sensitivity to chiral light, and the results show a substantial increase in the coupling strength between emitters and light.

Two-dimensional anti-de-Sitter spaces are the semi-classical counterpart to the $c=3$ Liouville theory and are found within the context of two-dimensional string theory, specifically the $(d, g)$ minimal model, after the application of $c=3$ Liouville action and certain boundary conditions. These classical solutions encompass the $c=3$ semi-classical spectrum. They are characterized by a unique thermodynamic property in which the specific heat is negative. These anti-de-Sitter spaces are distinguished from three-dimensional Schwarzschild anti-de-Sitter spaces, primarily due to differences in their universal horizons and infinite distances. These classical solutions can be visualized as projective hypersurfaces within the five-dimensional Euclidean space. These classical solutions may also be linked to the $c=6$ super Liouville theory.

Researchers investigating the Alcubierre warp drive have proposed a range of matter and energy configurations that could potentially implement the concept, with various forms of exotic matter and energy required to achieve stable solutions. Our paper presents a class of exact solutions to the Einstein equations in a flat spacetime with a warp drive, using a perfect fluid with negative pressure as the matter source. The warp drive metric exhibits a form of cylindrical symmetry similar to the Alcubierre metric, with both spacelike and time-like forms of the warp drive region possible. The necessary conditions for the warp drive region to be spacelike or time-like have been analyzed, with special emphasis on the stability issues. Our findings suggest that stable warp drive regions can be achieved with specific relationships between the metric parameters, indicating a promising approach to achieving stable warp drive solutions.

The increasing complexity of urban underground infrastructure systems necessitate a more structured approach to manage and plan these networks effectively, combining engineering and urban planning principles. The GUIDES framework, developed to address this need, utilizes multi-objective optimization to balance and prioritize various factors influencing these systems at large scales. The framework's effectiveness focuses on its applicability to smaller, more specific settings, and this study examines its applicability to a real-world urban tunnel emergency access problem through a literature review and case study analysis of a particular city. The results show that by integrating the GUIDES approach into urban planning, cities can optimize their underground infrastructure to meet specific operational requirements.

A two-dimensional Coulomb crystal consisting of 38${}^{20}$Ne$^{+}$ ions has been arranged in a Penning trap, with its electric field monitored via capacitance measurements. In this setup, the kinetic energy of the ions has been carefully regulated and maintained at a minimal level. Ambient conditions surrounding the trap have been evaluated by analyzing the ions' shell oscillations. This technique enables the detection of ambient heat transfer between the ions and surrounding electrons, thus quantifying the ambient heating rate. A customized ion-trap scanner has been designed for scanning the trap's electric field, which includes a rotating mirror to direct the image onto a charge-coupled device (CCD) camera for field analysis.

A key technique called tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS) uses a specially focused electromagnetic or chemical force to magnify local interactions at the point of contact. Combining both types of enhancement leads to novel, undetermined effects that can produce unique Raman signals. We've demonstrated this in our experiment by showing how combining electromagnetic and chemical effects with TERS can produce clear, distinct patterns in photoinduced mass spectra. Specifically, we've found that electromagnetic and chemical influences can be synchronized to significantly lower temperatures than previously thought possible. We've also found that the electromagnetic effect and chemical effect can be adjusted to cancel each other out, which has important implications for the development of TERS and other near-field spectroscopy techniques.

We conducted a search for anomalous microwave emission (AME) in five spiral galaxies through large-scale bolometer cameras and found no evidence of AME in our data. The data was taken at 90 GHz with a high angular resolution of 1.5 arcseconds and good signal-to-noise ratios. Our analysis focused on fields with known thermal dust emission and radio continuum emission in our data archive. The search for AME was done by comparing the spectral index between microwave and radio frequencies and by looking for emission at microwave frequencies that is not predicted by thermal dust models. Our data set includes fields with different signal-to-noise ratios and angular resolutions but did not yield any detectable AME. The lack of detection in our data set suggests that AME is primarily found in star-forming regions with high signal-to-noise ratios and high star formation rates. The search for AME in our data set was challenging due to the low angular resolution, which may have contributed to the lack of detection. Future searches for AME should be done in fields with high angular resolution and high signal-to-noise ratios.

A low-level entropy change associated with the  Free energy for the phase transition in ammonium sulfate arises primarily from entropic sources, as opposed to the primary enthalpic contribution observed in the corresponding barium sulfate system.

In a comprehensive experimental design, our goal was to examine the underlying cognitive processes involved in learning and choice behaviors, specifically in simple probability-based tasks. To this end, we developed a novel model of learning and choice, known as the Linear-Linex Model (LLM), which effectively explains a broad range of data from both pre-post experiments and choice tasks, including various forms of reinforcement learning, categorization tasks, and the development of preferences for European lotteries. Notably, our model suggests that people's initial response to loss is to lean towards stability, rather than an absolute aversion to risk, and that this initial response can be adjusted over time through increased sensitivity to new information. A key aspect of our model is its connection to the concept of psychological linex utility, which was first introduced by Rieger \& Calvert (2005). Through an analysis of parameters, our study provides insights into the underlying cognitive processes involved in learning and choice behaviors, and reveals several interesting patterns, such as a connection between risk tolerance and psychological linex sensitivity, as well as an integration of negative outcomes during learning.

The concepts of nonlocality and contextuality are deeply intertwined but not entirely synonymous in quantum mechanics. We propose a framework that allows us to compare the nonlocality of different state configurations by leveraging the framework of matrix operations. This framework helps us quantify contextuality and demonstrate various forms of nonlocality, including generalised nonlocality and intrastate nonlocality.

We propose a near-near-near-near neighbor (NNNN) approximation algorithm for searching in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space with $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximated accuracy, where the search time and preprocessing efficiency improve concurrently. For a given input set $P$ of $n$ points and a query $q$, if $d$-dimensional distances between $P$'s points and $q$'s nearest neighbors are greater than a certain threshold, the algorithm rapidly determines this threshold. Conversely, if the threshold is exceeded, the algorithm efficiently identifies $q$'s $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximated nearest neighbors. This NNNN algorithm achieves improved performance over its predecessors in two key areas: (1) faster preprocessing times with $O(n \log^d n)$ time complexity, and (2) more efficient query times with $O(\log^d (n/\varepsilon) \cdot \log_2 \log_3 \ldots \log_{d+1} (n/\varepsilon))$ time complexity. These advancements mark a significant milestone in its domain.

Unfolding, a method used to correct for measurement biases, is crucial in quantum computing experimentation.  The traditional iterative Bayesian unfolding technique is computationally expensive due to the complexity of updating probability distributions and selecting future measurements.  The high cost is attributed to the exponential scaling of the Hessian matrix, which hampers its practical implementation.  However, recent advancements in quantum computing have led to the development of more efficient Riemannian unconstrained optimization techniques, which can efficiently mitigate errors on near-term quantum computers.  By adapting the Bayesian unfolding process and leveraging these new techniques, the computational cost can be significantly reduced to linear scales.  The proposed algorithm achieves this by constraining the search space and utilizing a limited data set, making it more efficient without compromising its accuracy.  The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations, which show that it produces results comparable to the Bayesian unfolding technique while achieving substantial improvements in computational efficiency.

To explore the boundaries of human-robot collaboration, we propose a framework for training robots from user-provided instructions when specific task elements are inaccessible. Our approach involves adjusting existing training methods to account for situations where certain input values are unknown, effectively making some data points inaccessible. We test this framework on both actual robots and within a simulated environment, evaluating the effectiveness of different models and scenarios. Our results demonstrate that limiting access to some data points significantly reduces user efficiency when interacting with a robot, and even more so when the robot's task mapping becomes apparent. Our experiments also indicate that incorporating information about missing input values can substantially improve models trained to adapt to these situations, both in terms of overall performance and generalization to similar tasks.

Global metric maps like OctoMap effectively represent 2D environments for robot navigation, but they are not suitable for tasks requiring semantic PCP (point cloud and pose) information. In our research, we introduce HiTMap, a new representation that efficiently navigates 2D environments with minimal storage requirements. HiTMap is an adaptive metric map designed to handle point cloud data, dynamic objects, and sensor information. It differs from the cell-based global metric maps by utilizing a graph structure to represent nodes and edges. This graph is constructed using a k-d tree, where each node's value represents the estimated target point. HiTMap weighs navigation efficiency over global map completeness, and when the robot encounters a new location, it prioritizes acquiring a new graph node over revisiting previously mapped areas. In contrast to other representations, HiTMap does not rely on probability or gradient-based methods. Instead, it employs a binary HiTMap value to determine whether a target is within the map's bounds. This approach simplifies implementation while maintaining real-time capabilities. Our results show that HiTMap is an efficient method for 2D environment mapping, where it outperforms other representations in both storage requirements and real-time efficiency.

A novel approach has been developed to create a two-dimensional Z-complementary array code set (ZCACS) using a specific type of generalized Boolean function, where each input vector results in a unique binary output vector with distinct weights. Unlike traditional Boolean functions, these functions can produce output vectors of different weights, with at least $p-q+1$ and $2p-q-1$ $p$ and $q$ binary values respectively, given that $p>q$ and the output vector has $2p$ binary values. This novel approach enables the design of a 2-D ZCACS by employing a specific type of multi-valued generalized Boolean function, where each input vector $(x,y)$ results in a unique binary output vector $(a,b)$, with $a$ and $b$ having different weights. Utilizing this novel approach, a 6 $\times$ 8 2-D ZCACS has been designed, with a size reduction of up to 52% compared to the best known code set in the literature. Additionally, a 2-D ZCACS construction method has been proposed for $M=p \times q$, where $M$ represents the size of the 2-D code matrix. This novel approach can be used to create a 2-D ZCACS with a specific number of codewords, where each having $k_1$ and $k_2$ binary values, with $k_1> k_2

A novel learning approach is introduced for low-dose CT to mitigate the limitations imposed by non-Gaussian noise in X-ray detectors, which produce images contaminated with Poisson and Gaussian noises during the scanning process. To address this problem, two deep learning models are proposed: the first one utilizes a deep white Gaussian noise model to minimize the effect of non-Gaussian noise and results in an approximately Poisson-distributed low-dose CT image, while the second model leverages this low-dose image to generate a noise-reduced image. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed technique in producing high-quality images with reduced noise from Poisson and Gaussian sources.

The effective gap width model, a method of predicting light scattering through percolation, demonstrates greater accuracy than the locally applied effective medium theory and hence yields a more precise description of light propagation. This is particularly evident in cases where the medium's structure gives rise to complex, non-repeating patterns of connected pores and solid material. Effective gap width model predictions for light scattering can be calculated and compared to experimental results for percolating systems composed of pores embedded in a solid material. Moreover, this model can also be applied to systems where the pore phase encompasses the continuous medium, with the solid material forming the dispersed phase. In such cases, the model's predictions for light transmission are similarly compared to experimental findings. Notably, both the effective gap width and effective pore models provide a straightforward means of calculating the optical properties of percolating systems without the need to resolve their complex microstructure.

Contextual Named Entity Retrieval aims to swiftly and efficiently gather user context and relevant entity information from freely available text sources. Current CNER systems typically rely on pre-existing knowledge from information extraction databases such as Wikipedia, which can result in biased entity sets that may not align with users' actual interests. To address this limitation, our proposed system, named Context-Aware Entity Retrieval, aims to remove the constraints of pre-existing databases and allow users to provide feedback in a variety of ways (e.g., liking, disliking, rating on a scale), and dynamically adjust the model to learn users' preferences. Our approach is unique in that it can handle users' diverse preferences and provide real-time entity recommendations using a contextual framework that combines user feedback, entity similarity, and context relevance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing CNER systems in entity retrieval tasks and user studies show high user satisfaction rates with the recommended entities.

The widespread use of temporal plots has been attributed to their ability to convey complex data efficiently. Although often employed to illustrate system performance or research findings, temporal plots can be displayed alongside other visualizations. However, current methods fall short in addressing how these links should be implemented. In response, we have developed a general framework that enables us to create seamless interactions between temporal plots and other display types, such as maps and three-dimensional visualizations. This framework utilizes a versatile interface to design temporal plot layouts, allowing us to integrate interactive elements like hover-over effects. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through its application to a multi-scale visualization system utilized by the Large Hadron Collider's particle accelerator operators.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have led to their successful application across various real-world tasks by modeling complex relationships between entities. However, when it comes to integrating Electronic Health Records, which comprise unstructured, heterogeneous graph data, standard graph neural networks face a major challenge due to their lack of design specifically for handling and learning on high-dimensional, noisy, and multi-modal data. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called Meta-EHRNet, which leverages meta-learning to develop a unified representation for node features across different types, while also incorporating a self-attention mechanism to adapt to varying feature importance. By doing so, we enable the development of a more robust and scalable model for EHR analysis, as demonstrated by our experiments, which show that Meta-EHRNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art models for multiple tasks, including diagnosis and treatment outcome prediction.

We studied a system consisting of a monovalent electrolyte solution near a model soft charged surface using molecular dynamics simulations. The soft charged surface was modelled using a modified Lorentz-Berthelsen potential, imitating a typical charge density fluctuation on a charged surface. The potential's parameters were adjusted to mimic properties of systems such as graphene oxide, as well as charged mica and silica surfaces. The simulations examined how variations in ionic size, shape, and electrokinetic properties, polarization of ions and surface, and surface charge density fluctuations affected the electrolyte properties. The results showed that as ionic size increased, the electrolyte properties shifted towards a weaker coupling regime, characterized by a more uniform ionic distribution near the surface. The simulations also revealed that the electrostatic potential and surface charge density were in equilibrium, with the latter being sensitive to the choice of ionic size and shape. The study demonstrated that increasing ionic size, spherical shape, and high ionic polarization led to a more Gaussian-like ionic distribution near the surface, whereas a non-spherical ionic shape resulted in a distribution characterized by a longer tail compared to a Gaussian distribution.

To improve the extraction of software requirements from developmental source code, we've investigated using neural networks as an advanced approach. Given that pre-trained neural models like BERT demonstrate exceptional performance in various NLP tasks, we've evaluated BERT's effectiveness in extracting requirements from source code. We've found that BERT outperforms other models, such as fastText and ELMo, when applied to three distinct systems. We've also assessed the impact of tokenization methods on extracting requirements from Java methods using three systems, finding that a method combining identifier and tokenization based on rules yields better results than other methods.

This paper explores the optimization of energy consumption, spectrum allocation, and transmission time in multi-user relay communication systems, leveraging both fixed and mobile relays. To achieve this, the problem is cast as a complex optimization challenge, factoring in relay scheduling, power allocation, and time division. An iterative solution is proposed, utilizing alternating optimization and iterative clustering techniques, resulting in a feasible algorithm. Performance evaluation, conducted using Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrates the proposed solution's efficiency in reducing energy consumption while enhancing system performance.

The positions of YS-R state peaks in graphane are significantly influenced by the presence of magnetic impurities or impurity pairs, even when the spin-orbit coupling is considered. By neglecting these effects, some YS-R state peaks appear at $0$ meV, which is an underestimate. Upon the inclusion of spin-orbit effects, these unbounded peaks split into two, with their new positions accurately predicted by $\gamma$ and $\gamma_z$, parameters that describe the interaction between graphane's $p$ orbitals and a magnetic impurity or impurity pair.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has completed a data analysis for a specific decay process involving a kaon converting into a pion, a neutrino, and an antineutrino. Using 2019 data, the experiment set an upper limit on the decay's probability, finding no evidence for it at 2 standard deviations. Results show that the branching ratio for this decay is less than 7.0 x 10(-10), which is consistent with the Standard Model's prediction of 3.52 x 10(-9) with a 68% confidence interval.

This paper presents an innovative approach for down-sampling LIDAR point clouds to enhance the efficiency of data registration, particularly in complex environments containing both stationary and moving objects. By identifying critical points that contribute to accurate mapping, we developed a novel filter-based method for point cloud down-sampling. This technique initially locates the points with significant spatial variations, then selectively down-samples the others. When integrated with the Tight Coupled Multi-Swirl (TCMS) point cloud registration algorithm, our method significantly improves registration accuracy with down-sampled point clouds, yielding results comparable to those from dense registration. Notably, when applied to sequences featuring dynamic elements, such as a parking garage with moving vehicles, our approach significantly outperforms existing registration algorithms.

The vast information contained within satellite images holds significant value in understanding Earth's dynamics, yet the complexity and high dimensions of these images render them unsuitable for manual analysis. Consequently, there is a growing need for efficient and automated satellite image analysis. Deep learning techniques show great promise in this regard, but their practical applications are hindered by two major limitations. Firstly, these models are often too specialized and can only be trained on pre-labeled data, which is difficult to obtain. Secondly, these models are unable to generalize their findings across different satellite datasets. To overcome these challenges, researchers have turned to self-supervised learning methods, which can generate synthetic labels internally, reducing the need for pre-labeled data. In this study, a novel framework integrating multi-scale self-supervised learning and conditional generative models has been developed to address the limitations of previous approaches. This new method, Conditional Multi-scale Self-supervised Learning for Satellite Images (CM-SIL), has been tested using multiple satellite datasets and has consistently outperformed other state-of-the-art methods, including those using pre-labeled data, in building change detection tasks.

The dynamics of the non-linear absorption modification in a thin metallic nickel layer on a substrate is observed in high-fluence femtosecond laser irradiation. A theoretical model combining electron redistribution and laser intensity distribution accounts for the experimental findings. At lower fluences, the thin nickel layer exhibits a nonlinear increase in absorption, primarily due to surface energy-loss mechanisms. However, at higher fluences, the thick electron plasma generated inside the nickel layer produces a nonlinear decrease in absorption, despite the surface plasma's contribution. By comparing experimental and simulated data, it is demonstrated that the electron plasma generated within the nickel layer is the primary factor contributing to the non-linear absorption modification observed.

Adversarial attacks have compromised the reliability of deep neural networks (DNNs), which are now essential in many real-world applications. To counter these attacks, researchers have turned to generative adversarial networks (GANs) as a means of restoring DNN reliability. Previous studies primarily focused on training both GANs and DNNs simultaneously using adversarial data, failing to utilize GAN capabilities for data generation and adversary training. Conversely, this paper develops a framework that harnesses the potential of both GANs and DNNs to create robust DNN systems. By integrating DNN training with synthetic data produced by GANs, which are in turn guided by DNN parameters, the proposed method significantly enhances DNN resilience against adversarial attacks. Experimental evaluations on multiple attack methods demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach against a range of adversarial perturbations.

Segmenting multiple sclerosis lesions from MRI scans can be a complex task, 
especially when relying solely on in-house data, as the accuracy of automatic 
lesion segmentation tools can vary significantly from one hospital to another. 
One potential solution to this issue is the use of experience replay, a technique 
commonly applied in the field of reinforcement learning. By incorporating the 
knowledge gained from previous interactions, typically involving the labelling 
of past experiences, it is possible to adapt to new environments. Our study 
involved the development of an experience replay method for the segmentation of 
MS lesions. By combining the knowledge of multiple agents, specifically the 
BCNN and BCNN-RF models, it was possible to achieve adaptation to new data. Our 
results show that the experience replay method was able to adapt to data from 
three different hospitals, while the BCNN and BCNN-RF models were only able 
to achieve comparable results for data from the same hospital. Our findings 
suggest that the experience replay method provides a promising approach for the 
segmentation of MS lesions.

We introduce a novel approach for comparing metrics, characterized by a condition of transitivity over continuous optimal transport. This comparison principle encompasses metrics related to Wasserstein distance, its fractional variants, and other related metrics. By establishing this connection, we demonstrate the continuity of optimal transport with respect to these metrics. Furthermore, our metric comparison framework also encompasses more general comparisons involving convex risk measures. Key properties resulting from this comparison include the joint continuity of optimal transport, its convergence, and the existence of transversal processes.

Hybrid machine learning models are increasingly being explored to integrate knowledge from multiple sources, but there's a lack of clarity on how to incorporate knowledge that may not be certain or complete. This research delves into these uncertainties, developing new hybrid algorithms that balance data-driven and model-driven approaches, focusing on domain knowledge that's likely to be imperfect. The proposed algorithms are evaluated on surrogate-based optimization tasks, where they demonstrate improved efficiency and robustness over purely data-driven models. The results also highlight the significance of domain knowledge in enhancing a model's robustness against adversarial attacks, underscoring the potential of hybrid algorithms in building resilient intelligent systems.

The formation of massive stars is a complex and poorly understood process due to the limited availability of data. Studies on core collapse have traditionally relied on single-dish telescopes, which often lack the resolution needed to follow the evolution of individual cores. Our recent discovery of the most massive molecular core in W51 complex, detected by the Submillimeter Array, allows us to track the evolution of a massive core as it undergoes core collapse. Our mass calculation, based on the core's continuum emission, indicates a mass of approximately $5.9\pm1.3$ million solar masses. This is the first time a massive core has been directly observed using an interferometer, providing an opportunity to refine our understanding of massive star formation. Our high angular resolution observations reveal the morphology of dust emission at 850 $\mu$m and confirm the existence of a massive star candidate associated with the MM1 core. They also show that the star candidate is positioned at the center of the core and surrounded by a compact dust disk. Furthermore, the observations allow us to differentiate between free-free emission and dust emission and demonstrate that the radio jet from the massive star candidate has a significant impact on the surrounding core. Finally, the observations provide insights into the relationship between massive star formation and core collapse and highlight the importance of high angular resolution observations in this process.

Researchers anticipate that around two thousand times more microlensing events caused by primordial black holes than those caused by evolved stars have occurred in the Galactic bulge since the start of gravitational microlensing research in 1995. Assuming an average primordial black hole mass of thirty solar masses, it's estimated that approximately two such events have occurred each year. This prediction, however, relies on specific parameters including the fraction of primordial black holes within the Galactic bulge and their mass distribution. To identify primordial black holes within the Galactic bulge, scientists propose employing microlensing events combined with spectroscopic follow-up observations of associated baryonic counterparts. Moreover, future microlensing experiments are expected to detect these rare events more effectively, with the potential of identifying up to ten PBH microlensing events each year. This strategy could allow researchers to determine the cosmic abundance of these primordial black holes, constraining theories such as dark matter consisting of primordial black holes, with constraints potentially tightened to the level of a few percent.

We investigate the polar phase of hard spheres using numerical simulations to determine the phase's shape and volume fractions. Two previously unknown polar phase structures, a rhombohedral and a tetragonal phase, were discovered at packing densities higher than 0.5, in addition to the previously identified body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) polar phases. The phase diagrams of the BCC and FCC polar phases are examined, with a focus on understanding how they compare to their non-polar counterparts. The BCC phase is found to exist between $0.491 < \eta < 0.550$, with the FCC phase existing above $\eta \approx 0.550$. The BCC phase displays two sub-regions, with the first occurring between $\eta \approx 0.491$ and $0.515$ and the second between $0.515 < \eta < 0.550$. The BCC phase's sub-region characteristics were found to be similar to the FCC phase's features, with the FCC phase existing only above $\eta \approx 0.550$. The BCC phase's sub-regions correspond to distinct helical superstructures, with the first displaying $5 \times  0 \times h$ and the second $5 \times 5 \times h$ helices. The BCC and FCC phase structures were found to exist up to $\eta \approx 0.64$ and $0.68$,

Pretrained language models have become the new standard for natural language processing tasks. Although widely used, their actual workings are still somewhat mysterious. This study aims to shed light on the role of special tokens in these models by investigating their impact on the performance of RoBERTa on three tasks: sentiment analysis, noun phrase extraction, and text classification. The results indicate that removing special tokens results in acceptable performance in the sentiment analysis and text classification tasks, but causes significant degradation in noun phrase extraction. Additionally, our findings suggest that pretraining with a smaller vocabulary can lead to comparable performance as pretraining with a larger vocabulary, which is a more computationally efficient process.

The problem of determining the value of additions to a set has been studied under various network settings, and this study examines a specific scenario involving a Zernike light wave network. By analyzing the phase differences between pairs of arms, it is demonstrated that this problem can be effectively addressed using a simple neural network, trained on the coefficients of double zonal polynomials. The proposed solution achieves better results compared to a more complex deep neural network in terms of error metrics and computational efficiency.

Using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the characteristics of a specific type of glass-forming substance, propylene glycol, and demonstrate the applicability of thermodynamic scaling to its dynamics.
We verify that the ratio of its shear stress to its entropy follows a time-invariant plateau at low temperatures, consistent with prior claims in the context of sugars and disordered silica.
Conversely, the autocorrelation of its intermediate structural relaxation times fails to reach a stable plateau at low temperatures, contradicting a related hypothesis.
To eliminate any potential influence of propylene glycol's structure and its non-polar nature, we replicate our study using the simulation model representing a diverse set of liquids in the form of a flexible molecule consisting of only carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen atoms.
The results of these simulations provide a fundamental understanding of the characteristics of a system in the state of global rigidity and its dynamics in the context of thermodynamic scaling.

This paper delves into the performance of current NLI datasets with regard to sentences that differ in meaning, using various NLI datasets with increased label categories to examine the ability of models to infer nuanced differences. The study divides the NLI dataset into three categories based on the degree of meaning divergence: "contradictory", "opposite", and "neutral". The analysis shows that prominent transformer models achieve higher accuracy rates on "neutral" sentences, indicating a better understanding of meaning preservation, whereas they are more susceptible to "contradictory" sentences. Notably, the accuracy rates for "contradictory" and "neutral" sentences are similar for the BERT-KM model, which uses knowledge masking to improve the model's ability to infer contradictory meaning relationships. The study's findings highlight the need for further research to address the NLI task's challenges in handling contradictory meaning relationships.

We've observed a trend in recent NMT research where future inputs and outputs are
considered to handle tasks like reference-based evaluation and where named entity
extraction is applied successfully. However, incorporating a look-ahead attention
mechanism poses significant difficulties as it involves knowing the translation of unseen
text. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an attention mechanism that uses
language models to predict the translation of unseen text. This mechanism uses a neural
network to directly predict attention weights. We've also conducted experiments to
investigate how to implement look-ahead attention in a way that's efficient in terms of
parameters and computation. We've found that incorporating look-ahead attention
results in better performance on WMT14 English to German and newstitlenews datasets.

This paper focuses on the geometry of cotangent bundles and the associated differential operators, which arise from expressing curvature weights in a symplectic basis. The investigation of Fuchsian systems on cotangent bundles reveals novel differential operators and a distinct differential operator that uniquely characterizes symplectic geometry. The paper also establishes a characterization of the Weyl component, related to a specific Fuchsian system, in comparison to its real analog. The study further considers connections to two-dimensional topological quantum field theories and the spectral curves of the Kadomzev-Petviashvili hierarchy.

A universal change in thermal entropy of a CFT in three dimensions is noted as the conformal symmetry is collectively broken with varying degrees of non-conformal parity. In systems consisting of $N$ bosons or $N$ fermions interacting via an irrelevant scalar field, the thermal entropy initially remains $O(N)$ at high temperatures before shifting by an amount proportional to $\Gamma^2 N$, where $\Gamma$ represents the real-time distance from the conformal point and fermion/boson distinctions fall within $O(N)$ factorization.

This research presents a new approach to solving linear systems of equations with matrix-valued functions, which are also used to calculate pricing functions for various Asian options. By applying this method, we derive a solution for pricing options of type Advanced Lookback Options, which involves obtaining a solution to a system of equations using matrix single Laplace transforms. This solution enhances existing results by providing greater efficiency, specifically a reduction in computational complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2) with an improved logarithm dependence. Additionally, our approach allows for a parallel computing advantage. Furthermore, we extend the results to include double Laplace transforms, providing a parallel computing advantage of O(m/n) where m represents the number of parallel computations.

The Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope has helped identify numerous blazars through its gamma-ray observations. Yet, researchers are still unsure how these objects contribute to the diffuse gamma-ray background (DRB) on larger scales. To address this, a study was conducted to estimate the DRB generated by clusters of galaxies hosting blazars. By analyzing Fermi data on nearly 500 extended DRB sources, researchers simulated the characteristics of these objects. They also calculated the DRB contribution from typical extended sources, finding that the actual spectrum is softer than expected. Furthermore, first-generation Fermi data suggest that the DRB is dominated by extended sources, not point-like sources. Although the DRB spectrum remains undetermined, the data indicate that the DRB is primarily contributed by extended sources. However, the actual spectrum may be different due to potential biases in the Fermi data.

In the context of inflation driven by a complex scalar $\phi$, with a polynomial potential, sharp features are detected when the potential has discontinuities in derivatives. This is particularly true in scenarios where the scalar potential has breaks or kinks. Using an analytical approach, with a two-folded potential with singular derivatives, the impact of these sharp features on the parameters of non-Gaussianity is evaluated. By differentiating the potential, the two-slope form of $V(\phi)$ is obtained, and equation of motion for $\phi$ is established. Subsequently, using the three-point correlation function of scalar perturbations $f_{\phi\phi\phi}$, a constraint on the difference in slopes is derived, under the assumption of constant slow-roll. This results in a limit on the difference in slopes, $\vert\vert dV/d\phi\vert\vert_{\rm sup} \vert/\vert d^2V/d\phi^2\vert_{\rm av} \approx 4\times 10^{-3}$. Additionally, using the parameters of the background field $\phi$ and its derivative $\dot{\phi}$, a constraint on the break magnitude is obtained, yielding a limit of $ \vert\vert\dot{\phi}\vert\vert_{\rm sup} \approx 2.5\times 10^{-3}$.

This research proposes an innovative method to produce a clear and concise written explanation, illustrating the key features of the convolutional neural network representations it's based on. By employing the Visual Semantic Explainer, our algorithm, called LaViSE, populates an argumentation structure with semantically relevant information, enabling an expert to create a written summary by selecting crucial representations and their defining characteristics. LaViSE's functionality is showcased through its application to a range of existing CNN architectures, as well as through the presentation of an integrated platform that facilitates human-computer interaction to produce human-written summaries.

Understanding how high-temperature superconductors work is a major challenge in physics. Researchers study the properties of superconducting materials at various temperatures to learn more about how high-temperature superconductors work. In particular, they compare the properties of one-dimensional and two-dimensional materials made from bismuthate and cuprate compounds because of their similar structure. Despite the differences in their two-dimensional behavior, which affects how electrons move, researchers find similar patterns in their experimental results. This suggests that the same mechanism that explains their one-dimensional behavior also explains their high-temperature superconductivity, which is likely to be a problem for those who think high-temperature superconductivity only works in certain contexts.

To gain insight into the process of accessing HIV care facilities, researchers used Google Maps to calculate travel time and cost to these facilities, integrating this data with economic and demographic data of South African townships as well as electronic health records and survey data collected from 291 individuals. Through multivariate analysis, it was discovered that individuals familiar with the travel time to these facilities tend to know their treatment likelihood, whereas those unaware of travel times rely heavily on local care center director's recommendation, wait for personal circumstances to change, or rely on external advertisements for healthcare services. Furthermore, it was observed that individuals utilizing a health transportation system tend to report longer total travel times compared to those using private or public transportation, yet report lower overall costs.

We've studied the changes in the magnetic properties of a layer made from a helical antiferromagnet with a twist, caused by a nearby magnetic impurity. Using microscopic simulations, we found that a stable pattern of spinning magnetic structures can form and break the natural mirror symmetry in this layer. When a small magnetic field is applied, it transforms into a more stable alignment of the spins. Interestingly, this more stable alignment can arise from a temporary and less stable spinning magnetic structure under certain conditions. Furthermore, as applied magnetic field decreases, the spinning magnetic structures can transform back into a uniformly aligned state. Our research also reveals that a similar process is possible in materials that have a helical antiferromagnet with a natural twist, as shown in the crystal structure of a certain metal called half-helical antiferromagnet (Ca$_3$RuO$_3$).

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor models have gained significant attention in recent years, particularly for analyzing large datasets of various types.  Initially proposed by LAM in 2010, these models have undergone substantial transformations since their introduction.  This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of certain HDFD models, highlighting both their practical uses and methodological advancements, with a special focus on models featuring singular AR structures, which the author deems particularly valuable and underdeveloped at present.  After presenting the basic framework and key identification and identifiability criteria for singular AR models, the discussion will delve into recent methodological developments, illustrated by numerous examples, with a focus on models featuring singular AR structures.  Additionally, the paper will address the current state of singularity order estimation and model selection issues.  Finally, the discussion will conclude with an exploration of future research directions and potential challenges associated with these models.

The primary objective of this research is to elucidate the connection between the proximal mapping of a bilinear function and its relationship with the solutions of an equilibrium problem. We demonstrate that under specified conditions, the proximal mapping's fixed points align with the equilibrium problem's solutions. This research further explores the structural characteristics of the proximal mapping's fixed points and its range. A numerical example is provided to illustrate and visually demonstrate the findings.

Deep learning's widespread success stems from its ability to identify complex, visually-based patterns in data. Predictive uncertainty methods have made progress in assessing a model's limitations, but often focus solely on visual characteristics and neglect other important aspects of AI systems, like robotic sensing capabilities. To address this, we developed a novel method to quantify uncertainty in a broader range of AI functions, like filtering and feature extraction. By applying Bayesian techniques to these processes, we extend uncertainty assessments to their derived products, such as raw data and features. Using this approach in a simple robotic system on the ATARI dataset revealed significant benefits, allowing our model to avoid fatal mistakes and perform similarly to an ideal, fully informed agent.

Understanding global magnetic field oscillations in stars and the solar cycle requires an in-depth knowledge of turbulent forces driving dynamo processes. Since simulations involving all aspects of turbulence are computationally expensive, simplified models are often employed, potentially with limited success. Our study aims to create a more comprehensive dynamo model by incorporating various forces from simulations of turbulent convection, which have been carried out using supercomputers for early-type dwarf stars. To achieve this, we developed an innovative framework for translating turbulent characteristics from simulations of different geometries and resolutions, allowing us to fill the knowledge gap for simulations that are no longer accessible due to advances in computational power. By applying this framework, we can create realistic magnetic field scenarios, even with smaller-scale simulations, and study the effects of different resolutions and domain sizes on global magnetic field patterns. These findings can be used to develop more accurate magnetic field models for a range of star types.

Using the ALMA-ENOCH program, we conducted high-resolution observations of HCN and CS line emissions towards the central part of NGC4945. Based on these observations, we found that the molecular mass outflow rate in the central region is very high, approximately $1.1\times 10^8\;M_\odot\;{\rm yr}^{-1}$. This very high rate suggests that the molecular gas within the central $20\;{\rm pc}$ is being expelled at an extraordinary velocity of about $700\;{\rm km\;s}^{-1}$, which is comparable to the gas in the nuclear region's cone-shaped shape. This further confirms that the nuclear region is part of an active outflow.
